Analogs of Jacobian conditions for subrings

Piotr Jędrzejewicz    Janusz Zieliński
Abstract

We present a generalization of the Jacobian Conjecture for mm polynomials in nn variables: f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where kk is a field of characteristic zero and m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}. We express the generalized Jacobian condition in terms of irreducible and square-free elements of the subalgebra k⁡[f1,…,fm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}]. We also discuss obtained properties in a more general setting – for subrings of unique factorization domains.

Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture asserts that if kk is a field of characteristic zero and polynomials f1,…,fn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] satisfy the Jacobian condition

jac⁡(f1,…,fn)∈k∖{0}\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\in k\setminus\{0\} (1)

(where jac\jac denotes the Jacobian determinant), then k[f1,…,fn]=k[x1,k[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}]=k[x_{1}, …,\dots, xn]x_{n}]. In terms of endomorphisms of the polynomial algebra k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]: if a kk-endomorphism φ\varphi satisfies the Jacobian condition

jac⁡(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xn))∈k∖{0},\jac(\varphi(x_{1}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n}))\in k\setminus\{0\}, (2)

then φ\varphi is an automorphism. For more information on the Jacobian Conjecture we refer the reader to van den Essen’s book [7].

In Section 1 we present and discuss the following generalization of the Jacobian Conjecture, denoted by JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k), where kk is a field of characteristic zero, nn is a positive integer, m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\} and jac\jac denotes the Jacobian determinant with respect to given variables:

”For arbitrary polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], if

gcd(jacxi1,…,ximf1,…,fm, 1⩽i1<…<im⩽n)∈k∖{0},\gcd\big(\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{m}}},\;1\leqslant i_{1}<\ldots<i_{m}\leqslant n\big)\in k\setminus\{0\}, (3)

then k⁡[f1,…,fm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}] is a ring of constants of some kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].”

This conjecture can be expressed in terms of polynomial homomorphisms (and algebraic closedness) in the following way:

”For every kk-homomorphism φ:k⁡[x1,…,xn]→k⁡[x1,…,xm]\varphi\colon k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\rightarrow k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}], if

gcd(jacxi1,…,ximφ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xm), 1⩽i1<…<im⩽n)∈k∖{0},\gcd\big(\jac^{\varphi(x_{1}),\dots,\varphi(x_{m})}_{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{m}}},\;1\leqslant i_{1}<\ldots<i_{m}\leqslant n\big)\in k\setminus\{0\},

then Im⁡φ\Img\varphi is algebraically closed in k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].”

One of the authors obtained in [12] a characterization of endomorphisms satisfying the Jacobian condition (2)(2), where kk is a field of characteristic zero, as mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free ones. De Bondt and Yan proved in [4] that mapping square-free polynomials to square-free ones is also equivalent to (2)(2). We can express it in terms of polynomials f1=φ⁡(x1)f_{1}=\varphi(x_{1}), …\dots, fn=φ⁡(xn)f_{n}=\varphi(x_{n}): condition (1)(1) holds if and only if all irreducible (resp. all square-free) elements of the ring k⁡[f1,…,fn]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}] are square-free in the ring k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. In Theorem 2.4 we generalize this fact for mm polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}. Namely, the generalized Jacobian condition (3)(3) is equivalent to each of the following ones:

Irr⁡k⁡[f1,…,fm]⊂Sqf⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn],Sqf⁡k⁡[f1,…,fm]⊂Sqf⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn],\begin{array}[]{l}\Irr k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}]\subset\Sqf k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],\\[4.30554pt] \Sqf k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}]\subset\Sqf k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],\end{array} (4)

where Irr\Irr and Sqf\Sqf denote the sets of irreducible and square-free elements of the respective ring. This fact is a consequence of a multidimensional generalization of Freudenburg’s lemma ([8]) obtained in Theorem 2.3. A presentation of succeding generalizations of this lemma can be found in the Intoduction to [13].

The above conjecture motivates us in Section 2 to consider the following properties for a subring RR of a unique factorization domain AA:

Irr⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A,Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A.\Irr R\subset\Sqf A,\quad\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A. (5)

In Theorem 3.4, under some additional assumptions, we express the second condition in a kind of factoriality:

”For everyx∈A,y∈SqfA,ifx2y∈R∖{0},thenx,y∈R."\text{{"For every}}\;x\in A,\;y\in\Sqf A,\;\text{{if}}\;x^{2}y\in R\setminus\{0\},\;\text{{then}}\;x,y\in R." (6)

We call a subring RR satisfying condition (6)(6) square-factorially closed in AA. In Theorem 3.6 we show that, under the same assumptions, square-factorially closed subrings are root closed.

1 A generalization of the Jacobian Conjecture for 𝒎m polynomials in 𝒏n variables

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. By k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we denote the kk-algebra of polynomials in nn variables.

Recall from [11] the following notion of a ”differential gcd” for mm polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}:

dgcd(f1,…,fm)=gcd(jacxi1,…,ximf1,…,fm, 1⩽i1<…<im⩽n),\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=\gcd\big(\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{m}}},\;1\leqslant i_{1}<\ldots<i_{m}\leqslant n\big),

where jacxi1,…,ximf1,…,fm\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{m}}} denotes the Jacobian determinant of f1f_{1}, …\dots, fmf_{m} with respect to xi1x_{i_{1}}, …\dots, ximx_{i_{m}}. For m=nm=n we have

dgcd⁡(f1,…,fn)∼jac⁡(f1,…,fn),\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\sim\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}),

for m=1m=1 we have

dgcd⁡(f)∼gcd⁡(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn),\dgcd(f)\sim\gcd\left(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\dots,\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\right),

where g∼hg\sim h means that polynomials gg and hh are associated. We put dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)=0\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=0 if jacxi1,…,ximf1,…,fm=0\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{m}}}=0 for every i1i_{1}, …\dots, imi_{m}, that is, f1f_{1}, …\dots, fmf_{m} are algebraically dependent over kk.

Let kk be a field and let AA be a kk-algebra. A kk-linear map d:A→Ad\colon A\to A such that d⁡(f​g)=d⁡(f)​g+f​d​(g)d(fg)=d(f)g+fd(g) for f,g∈Af,g\in A, is called a kk-derivation of AA. The kernel of dd is denoted by AdA^{d} and called the ring of constants of dd. For more information on derivations and their rings of constants we refer the reader to Nowicki’s book [15].

Consider the following conjecture for mm polynomials in nn variables.

Conjecture JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k). For arbitrary polynomials f1,…,fm∈k[x1,f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1}, …,\dots, xn]x_{n}], where kk is a field of characteristic zero and m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}, if

dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)∈k∖{0},\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})\in k\setminus\{0\},

then k⁡[f1,…,fm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}] is a ring of constants of some kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Recall Nowicki’s characterization of rings of constants ([16], Theorem 5.4, [15], Theorem 4.1.4, p. 47).

Theorem (Nowicki, 1994). Let AA be a finitely generated kk-domain, where kk is a field of characteristic zero. Let RR be a kk-subalgebra of AA. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) RR is a ring of constants of some kk-derivation of AA,

(ii) RR is integrally closed in AA and R0∩A=RR_{0}\cap A=R.

Let DD be a family of kk-derivations of a finitely generated kk-domain AA, where kk is a field of characteristic zero. It follows from Nowicki’s Theorem that the ring

AD=⋂d∈DAdA^{D}=\bigcap_{d\in D}A^{d}

is a ring of constants of some single kk-derivation of AA ([16], Theorem 5.5, [15], Theorem 4.1.5, p. 47).

Daigle observed ([6], 1.4) that condition (ii) of Nowicki’s Theorem can be shortened to the following form:

(iii) RR is algebraically closed in AA.

Now we see for example that conjecture JC​(2,3,k)\text{JC}(2,3,k) asserts that if polynomials f,g∈k⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in k[x,y,z] satisfy the condition

gcd⁡(jacx,yf,g,jacx,zf,g,jacy,zf,g)∈k∖{0},\gcd\big(\jac^{f,\,g}_{x,\,y},\jac^{f,\,g}_{x,\,z},\jac^{f,\,g}_{y,\,z}\big)\in k\setminus\{0\},

then k⁡[f,g]k[f,g] is algebraically closed in k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z].

Let us note some basic observations according to conjecture JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k).

Lemma 1.1.

JC​(m,n,k)\text{\rm JC}(m,n,k) implies the Jacobian Conjecture for mm variables over kk.

Proof.

Assume that JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k) holds and consider polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] such that jacx1,…,xmf1,…,fm∈k∖{0}\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}}\in k\setminus\{0\}.

In k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we have dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)=jacx1,…,xmf1,…,fm\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}}, so k⁡[f1,…,fm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}] is algebraically closed in k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] by JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k). Hence, k⁡[f1,…,fm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}] is algebraically closed in k⁡[x1,…,xm]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]. And then k⁡[f1,…,fm]=k⁡[x1,…,xm]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}]=k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}], because f1,…,fmf_{1},\dots,f_{m} are algebraically independent over kk. ∎

Now, recall from [14] and [17] that a polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] over a field kk is called closed if the ring k⁡[f]k[f] is integrally closed in k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. When char⁡k=0\cha k=0, a polynomial ff is closed if and only if k⁡[f]k[f] is a ring of constants of some kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] ([14], Theorem 2.1, [15], Theorem 7.1.4, p. 80). Necessary and sufficient conditions for a polynomial to be closed were collected and completed by Arzantsev and Petravchuk in [2], Theorem 1. Ayad proved ([3], Proposition 14) that a polynomial f∈k⁡[x,y]f\in k[x,y], where char⁡k=0\cha k=0, is closed if

gcd⁡(∂f∂x,∂f∂y)∈k∖{0}.\gcd\left(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x},\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)\in k\setminus\{0\}.

His proof can be generalized to nn variables (it was noted in [10], Proposition 4.2), so we obtain the following fact.

Theorem (Ayad, 2002). JC​(1,n,k)\text{\rm JC}(1,n,k) is true.

Remark 1.2.

The reverse implication in JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k) need not to be true if m<nm<n.

In this case n⩾2n\geqslant 2. As an example we may consider a polynomial f1=x12​x2∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1}=x_{1}^{2}x_{2}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and, if m>1m>1, polynomials f2=x3f_{2}=x_{3}, …\dots, fm=xm+1f_{m}=x_{m+1}.

We have

dgcd⁡(x12​x2,x3,…,xm+1)=gcd⁡(2​x1​x2,x12)=x1,\dgcd(x_{1}^{2}x_{2},x_{3},\dots,x_{m+1})=\gcd(2x_{1}x_{2},x_{1}^{2})=x_{1},

so dgcd⁡(x12​x2,x3,…,xm+1)∉k∖{0}\dgcd(x_{1}^{2}x_{2},x_{3},\dots,x_{m+1})\not\in k\setminus\{0\}.

On the other hand, k⁡[x12​x2,x3,…,xm+1]k[x_{1}^{2}x_{2},x_{3},\dots,x_{m+1}] is algebraically closed in k[x1,k[x_{1}, …,\dots, xn]x_{n}] as a ring of constants of a family of derivations

{x1​∂∂x1−2​x2​∂∂x2,∂∂xm+2,…,∂∂xn}.\left\{x_{1}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}-2x_{2}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}},\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{m+2}},\dots,\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\right\}.

2 Analogs of Jacobian conditions in terms of irreducible and square-free elements

If RR is a commutative ring with unity, then R∗R^{\ast} denotes the set of non-invertible elements of RR. An element a∈Ra\in R is called square-free if it cannot be presented in the form a=b2​ca=b^{2}c, where b,c∈Rb,c\in R and b∉R∗b\not\in R^{\ast}. By Irr⁡R\Irr R we denote the set of irreducible elements of RR and by Sqf⁡R\Sqf R we denote the set of square-free elements of RR.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. Consider arbitrary polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}. Let g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be an irreducible polynomial.

The following lemma is a natural generalization of [12], Lemma 3.1. For the proof it is enough to add the argument from the beginning of the proof of [13], Proposition 3.4.a with Q=(g)Q=(g).

Lemma 2.1.

For a given i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\} consider the following condition:

there exist s1,…,sm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn], where g∤si, such thatg|s1​d​(f1)+…+sm​d​(fm) for every k-derivation d of k⁡[x1,…,xn].\begin{array}[]{l}\mbox{there exist $s_{1},\dots,s_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]$, where $g\nmid s_{i}$, such that}\\ \mbox{$g\mid s_{1}d(f_{1})+\ldots+s_{m}d(f_{m})$ for every $k$-derivation $d$ of $k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]$.}\end{array} (∗)

a) Then g|dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) if and only if condition (∗)(\ast) holds for some i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}.

b) If, for a given i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}, condition (∗)(\ast) holds, then fi¯\overline{f_{i}} is algebraic over the field k⁡(f1¯,…,fi−1¯,fi+1¯,…,fm¯)k(\,\overline{f_{1}},\dots,\overline{f_{i-1}},\overline{f_{i+1}},\dots,\overline{f_{m}}\,).

Note the following consequence of Lemma 2.1 and [12], Lemma 3.2.b (where the polynomial ww can be obtained as irreducible).

Corollary 2.2.

If g|dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}), then g|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}].

The following theorem is a multidimensional generalization of Freudenburg’s lemma ([8]).

Theorem 2.3.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero, let f1,…,fm∈k[x1,f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1}, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁…,xn]\dots,x_{n}] be arbitrary polynomials, where m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}, and let g∈k[x1,g\in k[x_{1}, …,\dots, xn]x_{n}] be an irreducible polynomial. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) g|dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}),

(ii) g2|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g^{2}\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}],

(iii) g2|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g^{2}\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some square-free polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}].

Proof.

Implication (ii)⇒(i)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(i)} was already proved in the proof of [12], Theorem 4.1, (ii)⇒(i)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(i)}. Implication (ii)⇒(iii)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(iii)} is trivial.

(i)⇒(ii)\text{(i)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)} We combine the arguments from proofs of [12], Theorem 4.1, (i)⇒(ii)\text{(i)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)} and [13], Theorem 3.6 (⇒)(\Rightarrow). Assume that g|dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}). By Corollary 2.2, g|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]. We proceed like in [12], using a derivation d⁡(f)=jacxj1,…,xjmf1,…,fm−1,fd(f)=\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m-1},f}_{x_{j_{1}},\ldots,x_{j_{m}}} for arbitrary j1<…<jmj_{1}<\ldots<j_{m}, instead of dnd_{n}, and applying Lemma 2.1 instead of [12], Lemma 3.1.

(iii)⇒(ii)\text{(iii)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)} We apply the proof of [4], Theorem 2.1, OPENOPEN3)⇒2)3)\Rightarrow 2). Assume that g2|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g^{2}\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some square-free polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}], so w⁡(f1,…,fm)=g2​hw(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=g^{2}h, where h∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Then there exist polynomials w1,w2∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w_{1},w_{2}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] such that w=w1​w2w=w_{1}w_{2}, w1w_{1} is irreducible and g|w1​(f1,…,fm)g\mid w_{1}(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}). Then we proceed like in [4]. ∎

As a consequence of Theorem 2.3 we obtain the following generalization of [12], Theorem 5.1 and [4], Corollary 2.2.

Theorem 2.4.

Let A=k⁡[x1,…,xn]A=k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where kk is a field of characteristic zero. Assume that f1,…,fm∈Af_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in A are algebraically independent over kk, where m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}. Put R=k⁡[f1,…,fm]R=k[f_{1},\dots,f_{m}]. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

(i) dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)∈k∖{0}\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})\in k\setminus\{0\},

(ii) Irr⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Irr R\subset\Sqf A,

(iii) Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A.

The above theorem allows us call conditions (ii) and (iii) analogs of the Jacobian condition (i) for a subring RR.

Remark 2.5.

Conditions (ii) and (iii) of Theorem 2.4 can be expressed in the following way, respetively:

(ii) for every irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] the polynomial w⁡(f1CLOSE,w(f_{1}, …,\dots, OPENfm)f_{m}) is square-free,

(iii) for every square-free polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] the polynomial w⁡(f1CLOSE,w(f_{1}, …,\dots, OPENfm)f_{m}) is square-free.

3 Square-factorially closed subrings

We will present some basic observations concerning conditions (ii) and (iii) from Theorem 2.4 for a subring RR of an arbitrary unique factorization domain AA. Conjecture JC​(m,n,k)\text{JC}(m,n,k) motivates us to state the following open question.

A general question. Let RR be a subring of a domain AA such that

Irr⁡R⊂Sqf⁡AorSqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A.\Irr R\subset\Sqf A\quad\mbox{or}\quad\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A.

When RR is algebraically closed in AA?

Lemma 3.1.

Let AA be a unique factorization domain. Let RR be a subring of AA such that R∗=A∗R^{\ast}=A^{\ast}. Consider the following conditions:

(i) Irr⁡R⊂Irr⁡A\Irr R\subset\Irr A,

(ii) Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A,

(iii) Irr⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Irr R\subset\Sqf A.

Then the following implications hold:

(i)⇒(ii)⇒(iii).\text{\rm(i)}\Rightarrow\text{\rm(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{\rm(iii)}.
Proof.

(i)⇒(ii)\text{(i)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)}

Assume that Irr⁡R⊂Irr⁡A\Irr R\subset\Irr A and consider an element a∈Sqf⁡Ra\in\Sqf R. Let a=q1​…​qra=q_{1}\ldots q_{r}, where q1,…,qr∈Irr⁡Rq_{1},\dots,q_{r}\in\Irr R are pairwise non-associated in RR. Then, by the assumption, q1,…,qr∈Irr⁡Aq_{1},\dots,q_{r}\in\Irr A. Moreover, since A∗=R∗A^{\ast}=R^{\ast}, q1,…,qrq_{1},\dots,q_{r} are pairwise non-associated in AA.

(ii)⇒(iii)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(iii)}

Assume that Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A and consider an element a∈Irr⁡Ra\in\Irr R. Suppose that a=b2​ca=b^{2}c, where b∈R∖R∗b\in R\setminus R^{\ast} and c∈Rc\in R. Then a=b⋅(b​c)a=b\cdot(bc), where b,b​c∈R∖R∗b,bc\in R\setminus R^{\ast}, a contradiction. Hence, a∈Sqf⁡Ra\in\Sqf R. ∎

Recall that a subring RR of a ring AA is called factorially closed in AA if the following implication:

x​y∈R∖{0}⇒x,y∈Rxy\in R\setminus\{0\}\Rightarrow x,y\in R

holds for every x,y∈Ax,y\in A. The ring of constants of any locally nilpotent derivation of a domain of characteristic zero is factorially closed. We refer the reader to [6] and [9] for more information about locally nilpotent derivations.

Lemma 3.2.

Let AA be a unique factorization domain. Let RR be a subring of AA such that R∗=A∗R^{\ast}=A^{\ast}. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) Irr⁡R⊂Irr⁡A\Irr R\subset\Irr A,

(ii) RR is factorially closed in AA.

Proof.

(i)⇒(ii)\text{(i)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)}

Assume that Irr⁡R⊂Irr⁡A\Irr R\subset\Irr A and consider elements x,y∈Ax,y\in A such that x​y∈R∖{0}xy\in R\setminus\{0\}. Let x​y=q1​…​qrxy=q_{1}\ldots q_{r}, where q1,…,qr∈Irr⁡Rq_{1},\dots,q_{r}\in\Irr R. Then q1,…,qr∈Irr⁡Aq_{1},\dots,q_{r}\in\Irr A, so without loss of generality we may assume that x=a​q1​…​qsx=aq_{1}\ldots q_{s} and y=b​qs+1​…​qry=bq_{s+1}\ldots q_{r} for some a,b∈A∗a,b\in A^{\ast}. Since A∗=R∗A^{\ast}=R^{\ast}, we infer that x,y∈Rx,y\in R.

(ii)⇒(i)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(i)}

Assume that condition (ii) holds and consider an element a∈Irr⁡Ra\in\Irr R. Let a=b​ca=bc, where b,c∈Ab,c\in A. By the assumption, b,c∈Rb,c\in R, so b∈R∗b\in R^{\ast} or c∈R∗c\in R^{\ast}. Hence, b∈A∗b\in A^{\ast} or c∈A∗c\in A^{\ast}. ∎

Note the following easy fact.

Lemma 3.3.

Let AA be a domain, let RR be a subring of AA. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) R0∩A=RR_{0}\cap A=R,

(ii) for every x∈Rx\in R, y∈Ay\in A, if x​y∈R∖{0}xy\in R\setminus\{0\}, then y∈Ry\in R.

Theorem 3.4.

Let AA be a unique factorization domain. Let RR be a subring of AA such that R∗=A∗R^{\ast}=A^{\ast} and R0∩A=RR_{0}\cap A=R. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A,

(ii) for every x∈Ax\in A, y∈Sqf⁡Ay\in\Sqf A, if x2​y∈R∖{0}x^{2}y\in R\setminus\{0\}, then x,y∈Rx,y\in R.

Proof.

(i)⇒(ii)\text{(i)}\Rightarrow\text{(ii)}

Assume that Sqf⁡R⊂Sqf⁡A\Sqf R\subset\Sqf A and consider x,y∈Ax,y\in A such that y∈Sqf⁡Ay\in\Sqf A and x2​y∈R∖{0}x^{2}y\in R\setminus\{0\}. If x∈Rx\in R, then x2∈Rx^{2}\in R, and hence y∈Ry\in R by Lemma 3.3.

Now suppose that x∉Rx\not\in R and xx is a minimal element (with respect to a number of irreducible factors in AA) with this property. In this case x∉A∗x\not\in A^{\ast}, so x2​y∉Sqf⁡Ax^{2}y\not\in\Sqf A, and then x2​y∉Sqf⁡Rx^{2}y\not\in\Sqf R. Hence, x2​y=z2​tx^{2}y=z^{2}t for some z,t∈Rz,t\in R, z∉R∗z\not\in R^{\ast}. We can present tt in the form t=u2​vt=u^{2}v, where u,v∈Au,v\in A, v∈Sqf⁡Av\in\Sqf A. We have u2​v∈R∖{0}u^{2}v\in R\setminus\{0\}, so u∈Ru\in R by the minimality of xx. We obtain x2​y=z2​u2​vx^{2}y=z^{2}u^{2}v, where y,v∈Sqf⁡Ay,v\in\Sqf A, hence x=c​z​ux=czu for some c∈A∗c\in A^{\ast}. By the assumptions, c∈Rc\in R, so x∈Rx\in R, a contradiction.

(ii)⇒(i)\text{(ii)}\Rightarrow\text{(i)}

Assume that condition (ii) holds. Consider an element r∈Sqf⁡Rr\in\Sqf R. Suppose that r∉Sqf⁡Ar\not\in\Sqf A, so r=x2​yr=x^{2}y for some x,y∈Ax,y\in A such that x∉A∗x\not\in A^{\ast} and y∈Sqf⁡Ay\in\Sqf A. Since x2​y∈R∖{0}x^{2}y\in R\setminus\{0\}, we obtain that x,y∈Rx,y\in R. We have x∉R∗x\not\in R^{\ast}, so x2​y∉Sqf⁡Rx^{2}y\not\in\Sqf R, a contradiction. ∎

Definition 3.5.

Let AA be a UFD. A subring RR of AA such that the implication

x2​y∈R∖{0}⇒x,y∈Rx^{2}y\in R\setminus\{0\}\;\Rightarrow\;x,y\in R

holds for every x∈Ax\in A, y∈Sqf⁡Ay\in\Sqf A, will be called square-factorially closed in AA.

Recall that a subring RR of a ring AA is called root closed in AA if the following implication:

xn∈R⇒x∈Rx^{n}\in R\;\Rightarrow\;x\in R

holds for every x∈Ax\in A and n⩾1n\geqslant 1. The properties of root closed subrings were investigated in many papers, see [1] and [5] for example.

Theorem 3.6.

Let AA be a unique factorization domain. Let RR be a subring of AA such that R∗=A∗R^{\ast}=A^{\ast} and R0∩A=RR_{0}\cap A=R. If RR is square-free closed in AA, then RR is root closed in AA.

Proof.

Assume that RR is square-free closed in AA. Consider an element x∈Ax\in A, x≠0x\neq 0, such that xn∈Rx^{n}\in R for some n⩾1n\geqslant 1. Let n=2r​(2​l+1)n=2^{r}(2l+1), where r,l⩾0r,l\geqslant 0. Observe first that since (x2​l+1)2r∈R(x^{2l+1})^{2^{r}}\in R, then applying Theorem 3.4 we obtain x2​l+1∈Rx^{2l+1}\in R.

Now, note that xx can be presented in the form x=s02m​s12m−1​…​sm−12​smx=s_{0}^{2^{m}}s_{1}^{2^{m-1}}\ldots s_{m-1}^{2}s_{m}, where s0,…,sm∈Sqf⁡As_{0},\dots,s_{m}\in\Sqf A and m⩾0m\geqslant 0. We will show by induction on mm that the following implication:

x2​l+1∈R⇒x∈Rx^{2l+1}\in R\;\Rightarrow\;x\in R

holds for every x∈Ax\in A, x≠0x\neq 0. Let m>0m>0 and assume that the above implication holds for m−1m-1. Put t=s02m−1​s12m−2​…​sm−1t=s_{0}^{2^{m-1}}s_{1}^{2^{m-2}}\ldots s_{m-1}, so x=t2​smx=t^{2}s_{m} and x2​l+1=(t2​l+1​sml)2​smx^{2l+1}=(t^{2l+1}s_{m}^{l})^{2}s_{m}. If x2​l+1∈Rx^{2l+1}\in R, then t2​l+1​sml,sm∈Rt^{2l+1}s_{m}^{l},s_{m}\in R by Theorem 3.4, so t2​l+1∈Rt^{2l+1}\in R by Lemma 3.3. Hence, t∈Rt\in R by the induction assumption and, finally, x∈Rx\in R. ∎
